prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, in which atoms trapped at a magic wavelength reach fractional uncertainties of 10^-18 in the measurement of time

statement.case_for: I change my preferred configuration from B010 to B043, and I want to say plainly why, because it is not simply a head count. My first-round test was whether something was found in nature. Re-reading the exchange, I think the lattice clock passes it better than I allowed. The magic-wavelength condition is a clue that nature gave us: a perturbation that cancels by design, so that thousands of neutral atoms can be interrogated without Doppler or recoil shifts. The result has then been used to look at nature, with gravitational redshift resolved over millimetres, bounds on drifting constants and on dark-matter couplings, and agreeing frequency ratios between laboratories on several continents in Sr, Yb and Hg. That is confirmation of a kind IceCube cannot yet offer, because there is no second telescope of comparable sensitivity. Kroll and Olsson have convinced me that the 2005 comb and 2012 ion prizes honoured different inventions, and Lindroth's and Pearce's priority account (the concept is Katori's, the push to the accuracy frontier is Ye's) gives a two-name credit that I can defend without commissioning more history. I therefore propose a single-part prize, Katori and Ye, with the citation kept tied to the magic-wavelength lattice so that it does not read as a general award for timekeeping.
statement.case_against: I have not stopped believing that B010 is the more obvious discovery, and my remaining reservation about B043 is exactly Lindroth's and Johansson's: it is an extremely successful invention that refines a measurement, and no new phenomenon was found. If the committee wants the prize to mark a new window on the universe, B043 is the weaker choice. There are also real attribution costs: Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Hollberg, Hinkley and the ion-clock groups are left out, and Ye's name spans combs, clocks and molecules, so the wording must be narrow. The redefinition of the second has not happened, and I agree with Johansson, Kroll and Pearce that it is a policy decision and should not count as scientific support; the case must stand on reproducibility of 10^-18 clocks alone. Finally, I am giving up B010 largely because the attribution among Halzen, Karle, Yoshida and the AMANDA pioneers is unresolved, not because I think the discovery is doubtful, and that is a weaker reason than a scientific one.

responses.point: Pearce moved from IceCube to B043 because it has the least dispute over who did what, and said he would support IceCube in a later round if a reliable historical review of the roles can be obtained; he also notes the two cannot be combined within three people.
responses.response: I agree with the constraint, and it is what decides it for me: Halzen, Karle and Yoshida plus Katori and Ye is five people, and a Halzen-Karle pair plus Katori-Ye is four. We have to let one of them carry the year. I would rather carry the one whose credit I can defend from the record we have than gamble on an expert review that may not arrive. I do not want your preference for building consensus to stand in for the science, though, and I do not think it does: your own argument, a decisive experimental realisation reproduced for twenty years, is a scientific one. I also keep B010 as my first alternative and would ask the Secretary's office to start the historical review of AMANDA and IceCube now, so that the case is ready next year if it is not chosen this one.

responses.point: Lindroth reads the clock as a discovery about what a quantum system can be made to do when its perturbations are understood, and answers the overlap objection by keeping the citation narrow to the lattice-clock concept and its realisation.
responses.response: I accept the framing and I accept the narrow citation. My earlier hesitation, which you quote from my own file back to me, was that no new phenomenon was found. Your answer, that the lattice removes a perturbation by design and thereby makes new tests of redshift, constants and dark-matter couplings possible, moves me more than the claim of novelty would have, because those tests are clues from nature and not elegant theory. I do not fully dismiss the sceptic's reading and I have kept it in my case against. I also take your offer on priority: I would be content for the citation to say invention and realisation and to name neither Ye's combs nor molecules.

responses.point: Kroll argues that the magic-wavelength lattice is a distinct conceptual step because it gives a many-atom, Doppler-free clock in which the perturbation cancels by design, which neither the comb nor ion trapping gives, and asked Johansson whether his low ranking was merit or overlap.
responses.response: This is the argument that turned me. The comb counts optical cycles and the ion clock shows single-particle control, and neither produces the stability of many atoms together with accuracy at the 10^-18 level; the 1e-15 to 1e-18 step really is a consequence of the lattice. I also thank you for the sharp reply you gave me on B010: you are right that an attribution difficulty in a large collaboration is not a scientific objection, and I said as much in round 1, but it is a practical one that the committee must still resolve before signing. On priority, I share your request that the early record of Lemonde and Takamoto be checked, and I would want the expert to answer it before the citation is finalised.

responses.point: Olsson says she is not yet sure the committee has found the people who did the original work for IceCube, which for her is the decisive difference from the clocks, and she asks that the clock citation stay about the magic-wavelength lattice rather than precision timekeeping in general.
responses.response: I think your point about the original work is correct, and I take it as the answer to the question I posed to the experts about Yoshida. For IceCube the diffuse flux is a collaboration result built on AMANDA, the optical modules and the ice calibration, and we do not have a defensible two- or three-name allocation today. I agree entirely about the citation: it should say magic-wavelength lattice clocks, and should not drift into a lifetime-achievement flavour. Your question whether a narrow citation suffices or the pair should be broadened to cover Takamoto is open, and I would leave it to the priority reviewer; I would not widen beyond Katori and Ye unless that review says the first demonstration cannot be separated from Takamoto's, since three names is the limit and the clean story would be lost.

responses.point: Johansson says he would be willing to see IceCube as a serious competitor, perhaps even as a second part, if the Halzen-Karle-Yoshida question and the role of AMANDA can be settled, and that the citation for B043 should name the lattice and magic-wavelength concept.
responses.response: Thank you for being generous about IceCube, and I agree on the citation. On a second part, I would not support it this year: Katori and Ye already use two of the three allowed names, so a second part could have at most one person, and a one-name IceCube prize would be the most arbitrary option of all. Better to keep the two apart. I also agree that the redefinition of the second is not a criterion, and I have removed it from my case. Your own disclosure that you should recuse on B023 means the committee should record that in the final ballot, and I note that B023 has not been defended by anyone else in round 1.

responses.point: Mehlig prefers B020 for a simple universal mechanism, but accepts B043 as a strong, defensible outcome if the citation rests on the demonstrated lattice-clock concept and 10^-18 performance, and asks whether the committee equates unanimity of experimentalists with the strongest scientific case.
responses.response: I think your challenge is fair and I do not want to be counted among the experimentalists for the sake of it. The Halperin-Nelson-Young mechanism is elegant and I do not dispute the three-name credit, but I read the evidence the way Kroll does: the hexatic phase is established system by system, with colloids and films reaching different answers on whether the transition is first order, and the 2016 prize already covers the defect idea in Kosterlitz and Thouless. A citation would have to say exactly what was confirmed in nature, and I cannot write one that does so with confidence. The citation I propose for B043 rests, as you asked, on the lattice concept and the demonstrated 10^-18 performance, not on prospective applications.

responses.point: Eriksson asks whether the committee should reward a precision tool or a new state of matter, and notes the redefinition of the second has not happened, while Pearce and he agree the pairing mechanism and the absence of Yuan Cao are open issues for B029.
responses.response: The choice between a tool and a new state of matter is a genuine one, and I do not think it is obvious that clocks must outrank the moire discovery. My difficulty is that I am wary of elegant theory that nature has not yet fully confirmed, and for B029 the prediction was confirmed but the correlated phases remain without a settled mechanism, while the credit question about Yuan Cao is a real fairness problem that you and Pearce both raise. I would put B029 as my second alternative, because I think you may be right that it is one or two years from being ready, and that is a statement about timing and not about quality.

uncertainties: Whether the priority record supports Katori and Ye as the decisive pair, or requires a wider or different set of names (Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Hollberg and others); an outside expert should settle this before the citation is finalised.

Whether the committee will accept the lattice clock as a distinct invention and not a refinement of the 2005 and 2012 lines; I now think so, but the objection is real and I cannot rule out that it will outweigh the case.
How credit for IceCube would divide among Halzen, Karle, Yoshida and the AMANDA pioneers, which is the reason I set B010 aside this year and would want a historical review before any later year.
My knowledge of both the lattice-clock and the IceCube record is from memory and I have not verified the details.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for B043: Katori and Ye are not my supervisor (Gross), mentor (Rubinstein) or co-author (Van Riet). My preferred configuration no longer involves IceCube, which was the only candidate where my profile left open a possible connection through Uppsala colleagues; I would still disclose that if B010 returned, and I have no information either way. I am a string theorist and not an expert on atomic physics, and I rely on Kroll, Lindroth and Olsson for the priority record. Johansson's recusal on circuit QED does not touch my position.
